questions.problem: Consider the function $f(x)=12-6x$ and the point $P(3,-6)$ that lies on $y=f(x).$ Given that $f(x)$ is invertible in the vicinity of $P,$ determine the slope of $y={f}^{-1}(x)$ at the point $(-6,3).$
questions.worked_solution:
We start by calculating the derivative of $f$ at the point $(3,-6).$

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}f(x) & =12-6x \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =-6 \\ {f}^{′}(3) & =-6\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Since $(3,-6)$ lies on $y=f(x),$ we know that the corresponding point $(-6,3)$ lies on $y={f}^{-1}(x).$

Furthermore, the slopes of the tangents to the two respective points are reciprocals. Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}({f}^{-1})^{′}(-6) & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(-6))} \\  & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}(3)} \\  & =\frac{1}{(-6)} \\  & =-\frac{1}{6}.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
The following table gives the values of functions $f(x)$ and ${f}^{′}(x)$ at some points. Find $({f}^{-1})^{′}(0).$

| **$x$** | $f(x)$ | ${f}^{′}(x)$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $2$ | $4$ |
| $2$ | $0$ | $-1$ |
questions.worked_solution:
The formula for the derivative of the inverse is

$$
({f}^{-1})^{′}(x)=\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(x))}.
$$

Substituting $x=0,$ we have

$$
({f}^{-1})^{′}(0)=\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(0))}.
$$

From the table, we obtain ${f}^{-1}(0)=2$ and ${f}^{′}(2)=-1.$ Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}({f}^{-1})^{′}(0) & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(0))} \\  & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}(2)} \\  & =\frac{1}{(-1)} \\  & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Consider the function $f(x)=-3+5{e}^{x+1}.$ Given that $y=f(x)$ is invertible throughout its domain, determine $({f}^{-1})^{′}(2).$
questions.worked_solution:
To determine $({f}^{-1})^{′}(2),$ we use the following formula:

$$
{({f}^{-1})}^{′}(2)=\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(2))}
$$

First, we calculate the value of ${f}^{-1}(2).$ To do this, we solve the equation ${f}^{-1}(2)=x.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{-1}(2) & =x \\ f(x) & =2 \\ -3+5{e}^{x+1} & =2 \\ 5{e}^{x+1} & =5 \\ {e}^{x+1} & =1 \\ x+1 & =0 \\ x & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ${f}^{-1}(2)=-1.$

Now, we calculate ${f}^{′}(-1),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =-3+5{e}^{x+1} \\ {f}^{′}(x) & =5{e}^{x+1} \\ {f}^{′}(-1) & =5{e}^{0} \\ {f}^{′}(-1) & =5\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{({f}^{-1})}^{′}(2) & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}({f}^{-1}(2))} \\  & =\frac{1}{{f}^{′}(-1)} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$
